query: What explicit, observable decision rules will distinguish hearing, formulation, and comprehension trouble across speech, prosody, gaze, and gesture?

response.query: What explicit, observable decision rules will distinguish hearing, formulation, and comprehension trouble across speech, prosody, gaze, and gesture?
response.answer: Hearing trouble often involves difficulty in detecting sounds; formulation trouble involves issues in constructing speech; comprehension trouble involves difficulty in understanding spoken language. Prosody, gaze, and gesture help differentiate these by observing speech patterns, eye movements, and body language.

results.title: Frontiers | The Role of Gesture in Communication and Cognition: Implications for Understanding and Treating Neurogenic Communication Disorders
results.content: #### Speech and Language. # The Role of Gesture in Communication and Cognition: Implications for Understanding and Treating Neurogenic Communication Disorders. Gesture is a fundamental component of language that contributes meaningful and unique information to a spoken message and reflects the speaker’s underlying knowledge and experiences. We review a robust literature from the field of psychology documenting the benefits of gesture for communication for both speakers and listeners, as well as its important cognitive functions for organizing spoken language, and facilitating problem-solving, learning, and memory. We review the literature characterizing gesture production and its role in intervention for people with aphasia, as well as describe the much sparser literature on gesture in cognitive communication disorders including right hemisphere damage, traumatic brain injury, and Alzheimer’s disease. This review highlights several gaps in the field of communication disorders which may serve as a bridge for applying the psychological literature of gesture to the study of language disorders.

results.title: From age two, children use pronouns to predict who will speak next in conversation - ScienceDirect
results.content: # From age two, children use pronouns to predict who will speak next in conversation. By age 2;0 children use subject pronouns to anticipate upcoming conversational structure. We find no evidence that children use prosodic cues to anticipate upcoming conversational structure. Children’s and adult’s use of pronouns to predict upcoming speaker changes requires a semantically meaningful context. Earlier studies showed that in conversation, from around age 2;6 children who are watching a conversation are more likely to spontaneously switch their gaze to an upcoming responder when they hear a question compared to when they hear a non-question. Tracking the eye gaze behavior of Dutch children (1–4-year-olds) and adults, the purpose of this research was to examine whether participant’s predictions are driven by individually informative linguistic cues, comparing two cues associated with interrogatives: one lexical cue (subject pronoun) and one canonically associated prosodic cue (utterance-final intonation).
